summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's penal code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries a maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained at independence and carried into its first post-independence penal code, adopted in 2015, with an enhanced sentence. The 2023 US State Department country report records the criminalisation alongside societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons and a separate law making no gender distinction for assault.

The prohibition is applied to foreign nationals as well as residents. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, an Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government described him as a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local law including the penal code's prohibition. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one of them openly gay; Eritrea's ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action. The most recent documented expulsion in this record is from 2013; no later instance is documented.

Detention is used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, which is known for housing political prisoners and journalists. The most recent documented arrest of this kind in this record is from 2003; no later instance is documented. Reporting on those facilities records abuse, torture and beating of prisoners as commonplace and some illegal executions, although the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported that the death penalty was not used in 2013.

Openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and, on that basis, did not participate in the political process, according to the 2023 US State Department report. That report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by social stigma; in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programmes detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality. The government labels disloyal individuals "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles", a practice recorded in the 2011 US State Department report.

Criminalisation undermines health and care access. ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing that it makes prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern. There is no law banning conversion therapy; OutRight Action International found that conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma, and LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. There is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people; the UK Foreign Office recorded raising these concerns bilaterally and through the EU. The government rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review recommendation to legalise same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people", with no major efforts to change or rescind the existing law, and in 2010 Eritrea joined other African states in rejecting the Yogyakarta Principles.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern of state enforcement against foreign nationals sits inside a broader restriction of expression: the 2023 US State Department report documents no public LGBTQ organisations and tight limits on public expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, while the 2010 report for the same government records criminalisation together with societal stigma, torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service. Detention exposure for a person accused of same-sex conduct therefore occurs within a detention system whose conditions are independently criticised.

External advocacy has produced no change of law. The UK Foreign Office raised Eritrea's criminalisation and absence of anti-discrimination protection bilaterally and through the EU, and the government rejected a Universal Periodic Review recommendation outright on cultural grounds; Eritrea also joined other African states in rejecting the Yogyakarta Principles in 2010. The OutRight country overview, updated 12 March 2026, continues to record Article 310(1) with its seven-year maximum.

An unconfirmed 2002 UK refugee claimant account reports that gay men and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military were subjected to severe physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers; the account is a single unconfirmed source and no corroborating figure is recorded.

LGBTQ organisations cannot operate publicly: the 2023 report found none, and expression of sexual orientation and gender identity is tightly restricted, so residents cannot assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State-run radio and television aired programmes detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality in the early 2000s, and criminalisation is reported to make HIV prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult to run.

People suspected of same-sex conduct are held in detention facilities; six gay men arrested in Asmara in 2003 were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, which houses political prisoners and journalists, where abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is reported as commonplace.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory documents no gender-identity-specific offence, no rules on gender markers in passports or identity documents, no entry or visa screening provisions keyed to gender transition, and no facility or bathroom rules specific to trans visitors. Whether Eritrea's law reaches gender expression as such, distinct from the recorded prohibition on homosexual conduct, is not resolved by these sources.

No trans-specific violence statistic with a denominator appears in this record, so no trans-specific rate can be stated against Eritrea's general homicide rate. The military-abuse account rests on a single unconfirmed 2002 refugee claim, and the reported absence of the death penalty in 2013 is a single-year observation.

No youth-specific care findings are recorded. Enforcement documentation for arrests and expulsions stops at 2013 for expulsions and 2003 for arrests; the record does not establish whether such actions continue, and an undocumented present is not evidence of a safe one.
